big_idea: Modelling starts with a real-life situation. We notice it and ask MATH questions about it.
learning_intention: We are learning to describe a real-life situation and ask math questions about it.
student_learning_goal: I can describe a real-life situation and ask math questions about it.
success_criteria: I can describe what happens at the sugar bush in 2-3 sentences.
I can ask 3 math questions about the sugar bush.
I can explain why we want to ask math questions.
lesson_specific_materials: Modelling cycle chart (5 steps: situation, question, data, predict, reflect)
Per-pair set of paper maple trees
Lesson 1 situation tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: What is a sugar bush? What happens there? Maple opens with the unit refrain: 'HOW MANY? HOW MUCH? HOW LONG? HOW TALL? — that's a math question, every one!' (Class echoes.)
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Reveal Maple the Maple Tree mascot. 'Friends — meet Maple. Maple is a maple tree. Maple lives at the SUGAR BUSH. Today we'll think like math scientists about what happens there.'

'A sugar bush is a forest of maple trees. Every spring, people visit and TAP the trees — drill a small hole and put in a wooden spile. The tree's SAP drips out into a bucket. Then the sap is BOILED to make MAPLE SYRUP — the sweet topping for pancakes!'

'A sugar bush is a real-life situation. Today we ask: WHAT MATH QUESTIONS could we ask about the sugar bush?'

Brainstorm with the class. Take all questions. Examples:
- How many trees are in the sugar bush?
- How much sap does each tree make?
- How long does it take to boil sap into syrup?
- How many buckets do we need?
- How much syrup will we get?
- How much money is one jar of syrup?

Write each on the chart. 'These are MATH QUESTIONS. We can answer them by counting, measuring, predicting.'

Introduce the modelling cycle. 'When we ask math questions about a situation, we're MODELLING. The cycle has 5 steps: SITUATION, QUESTION, DATA, PREDICT, REFLECT. Today we're at the SITUATION + QUESTION steps.'

'Tomorrow we'll collect DATA. Day 3 we PREDICT. Day 4 we REFLECT. Day 5 you do your own modelling.'
student_actions: Brainstorm math questions about the sugar bush.

steps.instruction: Whole group: brainstorm 3 more sugar-bush questions. Sort questions by 'easy to answer' and 'harder to answer'.
steps.teacher_prompt: Lead the class to think about question difficulty.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Tree Counting — pair counts paper trees and asks 1 question about them. Station B: Real-Life Situation Cards — pair picks a card (recess, lunch, sports) and asks 3 math questions. Station C: My Sugar Bush — pair draws their own sugar bush scene and writes 3 questions.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: ask a question that requires PREDICTION (not just counting). Like 'how much syrup if we tap 10 trees?'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'Some questions need a guess. Find ONE.'

steps.instruction: Discuss: what makes a question 'mathematical'? It can be answered with NUMBERS or PATTERNS.
Circulate to record formative evidence on the situation tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Mark whether they asked 3+ questions.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: 2-3 pairs share their wonder-question lists. Class sorts each onto a chart: COUNT / MEASURE / PREDICT. Pairs debate which strategy fits each question best (e.g. 'how many trees?' = COUNT, 'how long is one tap?' = MEASURE, 'how much sap will tomorrow's bucket hold?' = PREDICT). Cite English (2003) primary mathematical modelling — children learn that math questions PARTITION naturally into operational families.
steps.teacher_prompt: Maple: 'Same wonder, different math. The QUESTION decides which tool — counting, measuring, or predicting — answers it.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only counting questions.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: ask 5+ questions including prediction questions.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-supported situation cards. Sentence frame: 'How many ___ are there?'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Walk around the classroom asking math questions about real things they see. NO-MATERIALS VERSION: skip the mascot and printed cards; point to any classroom plant or whiteboard sketch as Maple. Teacher orally names three classroom situations (snack, recess, lining up); children sketch their wonder-question on scrap paper. No printed materials required.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: describes a situation; asks 3+ math questions; explains why questions matter.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the situation tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: Why do we ask math questions about real life?
What's one math question YOU asked today?
Maple's preview: tomorrow Sap Sam shows us how to COUNT what we asked today (Lesson 2 — C4.1). Look at your sticky — would COUNTING answer it? Or do we need to MEASURE or PREDICT?
consolidation.exit_routine: Maple's refrain — class chants 3x: "HOW MANY? HOW MUCH? HOW LONG? HOW TALL? — that's a math question, every one!" Each child writes ONE math question on a sticky and tags it COUNT / MEASURE / PREDICT.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 captures the SITUATION + QUESTION steps of the modelling cycle. Children at L4 generate 3+ varied questions.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child asks 'How many maple trees are pretty?' — repairing the descriptive-vs-mathematical question confusion
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On real-life math posing, Grade 1 children frequently default to feeling-words ('I love sugar bush!') rather than answerable questions when invited to wonder. English (2003, 'Mathematical Modelling in the Primary School') and Lesh & Doerr's model-eliciting activities frame this as the question-vs-statement gap — children need explicit cueing that a math question is one whose answer is a NUMBER (count, measure, prediction).

Today's question-tagging task is the gateway to the rest of the unit: Lesson 2 counts what was asked today, Lesson 3 predicts based on Lesson 2 data, and Lesson 5's capstone runs a child-chosen modelling cycle end-to-end.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station C. The child writes 'How pretty is the maple tree?' as a math question.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Good question! But it's hard to answer with NUMBERS. Pretty is a feeling, not a count. Math questions need NUMBERS or PATTERNS.' Pause.

'Let's change it. What number could we ask about?' Lead them: 'How TALL is the maple tree?' (in metres). 'How many LEAVES?' 'How many BRANCHES?' Each is countable or measurable.

Write the rule. 'Math questions usually start with HOW MANY, HOW MUCH, HOW LONG, HOW TALL. They need a number to answer.'

If the child STILL asks descriptive questions: provide a sentence frame: 'How ___ is the maple tree?' with NUMBER-friendly words filled in (many, much, long, tall).

Long-term recovery: every brainstorm session highlights both types and gently moves toward the math.
expected_student_responses: (Mid) Recognizes math vs description with prompts.
(Strong) Auto-asks math questions starting with HOW MANY/MUCH.
(Stretched) Asks PREDICTION questions ('if we tap 10 trees, how much syrup?').
common_misconceptions: All questions are math questions. (Repair: math questions need numbers.)
Math is only counting. (Repair: math also includes patterns, measurement, prediction.)
You can't ask math questions about real life. (Repair: you can! Real life is FULL of math.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child uses pure feeling-words ('it's beautiful'): drop to a HOW MANY frame — 'great! Now ask HOW MANY beautiful trees are there?' Force a count-target into every wonder.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child uses numbers but no question word ('5 trees'): model 'How many ___?' / 'How long ___?' as a sentence stem; child rewrites as a question.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child writes good questions but forgets the math frame ('why are trees green?'): label categories on the chart — ASKABLE BY MATH (count/measure/predict) vs ASKABLE BY OBSERVATION.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C4 step 1 (situation + question).

parts_outline.task: Describe the sugar bush in 2-3 sentences.
Write 3 math questions about the sugar bush.
Pick a real-life situation from your day. Write 2 math questions about it.
